newsitem.title: UK: S&P affirms Pakistan foreign currency ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms Pakistan foreign currency ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Wednesday it affirmed the Islamic Republic of Pakistan's B plus long-term foreign currency and B short-term foreign currency credit ratings.
"The outlook is also affirmed at stable," S&P said in a statement.
The long-term rating and outlook apply to Pakistan's two U.S. dollar-denominated Eurobonds, totaling $300 million, S&P said.
S&P said ratings on Pakistan are constrained by:

"-- Heavy external debt burden and vulnerable external payments. Net external debt relative to exports is about 240 percent, by far the highest of any rated sovereign, and large amounts of foreign currency deposits leave external liquidity fragile. Current account deficits are large and will be pressured in coming years by high import demand, rising debt service, and the difficulty of expanding exports and lessening their high concentration in cotton.

-- Large fiscal deficit (6.3 percent of GDP in the year ending June 1996) -- reflecting a narrow tax base and inflexible spending on defense and servicing of a heavy public debt, which undermines monetary management and the balance of payments.
-- Serious political uncertainty that impedes fiscal adjustment and structural reforms.
Mitigating rating factors include:

-- Policy continuity, which has achieved major external, industrial and financial liberalization since 1988, enhancing economic potential. The economy is among the most open in the region, and foreigners and the private sector enjoy broad investment opportunities, as evidenced by Pakistan's very successful energy program. The December 1996 resumption of International Monetary Fund (IMF) lending should support further fiscal adjustment and structural reforms.
-- Comparatively strong economic growth and moderate inflation.
-- An unblemished debt service record," S&P said.
"Political strife, policy slippage and economic shocks have led to three foreign exchange crises in the past four years," S&P said.

The latest, which appears to have peaked in October 1996 with precariously low foreign exchange reserves, was driven by deteriorating confidence surrounding the Bhutto government's dismissal for economic mismanagement and corruption. Underlying factors included major fiscal slippage in the past two fiscal years and earlier this fiscal year, accompanying rapid credit growth, and slowing structural reforms including tariff and other tax reforms and privatisation, S&P said.

The caretaker government has adopted major stabilisation policies -- led by large fiscal adjustments (an expenditure-led cut in the budget deficit to 4 percent of GDP this fiscal year), exchange rate depreciation, higher interest rates and tighter credit policies -- and is preparing for ambitious banking and tax reforms and privatization for the government to be elected in February 1997.

"Barring major policy or political disruptions, the IMF's resumption of financial assistance should encourage private and other official capital inflows and reduce external liquidity pressures in coming months," S&P said.
Also expected this fiscal year is a lower current account deficit (to 5.6 percent of GDP), slower but continued economic growth (5 percent) and moderate inflation (11 percent), it said.
OUTLOOK: Stable.

"Ratings of Pakistan hinge on significant policy progress in 1997 -- especially in budget deficit reduction, tax and banking reform and privatization -- and confidence that the coming government can deliver on continued progress over the medium term," S&P said.
"Policy implementation will continue to be challenged by uncertainty over the strength of the next government and disruptive relations between political parties," S&P said.

"Potentially mitigating these uncertainties are the narrow policy differences between political parties, President Leghari's influential support of reform, and the lack of realistic alternatives," S&P said.
